item.title: MOV Elimination: Does it Really Have Zero Latency on Modern CPUs?
item.description:
“MOV Elimination: Does it Really Have Zero Latency on Modern CPUs?”

Does the MOV instruction truly offer zero latency on modern CPUs, or is it a nuanced behavior influenced by microarchitecture and specific instruction patterns? This exploration delves into the mechanics and observed performance impacts of MOV elimination, supported by practical assembly examples and benchmarking.

The core concept of MOV elimination, often referred to as register renaming for MOV, allows certain copy operations to bypass actual execution units. Instead, the operation is handled during the instruction issue or rename stage. This effectively removes the latency and execution port usage associated with a typical instruction.

item.title: Optimal x86 Assembly: TEST Reg,Reg vs. OR Reg,Reg vs. CMP Reg,0 for Zero Checks
item.description:
“Optimal x86 Assembly: TEST Reg,Reg vs. OR Reg,Reg vs. CMP Reg,0 for Zero Checks”

When performing zero checks in x86 assembly, you might encounter different instructions like TEST reg, reg, OR reg, reg, and CMP reg, 0. Do these choices significantly impact performance, and what are the nuances of each? Let’s dive into the technical details to understand which method is most effective.

The primary question is whether there’s a discernible performance difference when comparing a register against zero using these distinct instructions.

item.title: Troubleshooting Integer Overflow with x86 DIV Instruction
item.description:
“Troubleshooting Integer Overflow with x86 DIV Instruction”

When working with assembly language, particularly on x86 architectures, the DIV instruction is fundamental for performing division. However, a common pitfall that can lead to unexpected results, specifically integer overflow, is the improper management of the EDX register. This post delves into why this occurs and how to correctly utilize DIV for both signed and unsigned operations.

Why Does DIV Cause Integer Overflow?

The DIV instruction in x86 architecture operates on a 64-bit dividend formed by concatenating the EDX register with the EAX register (represented as EDX:EAX). This combined 64-bit value is then divided by a specified operand, typically another register or memory location.
